clue.text: Requirement for sporting types in GPs’ workplace

blocks.note: athletes need regular training sessions to stay sharp
a family doctor works in a general medical surgery of that name

explanation.surface: What athletes need, available at the local doctors' surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: Two unrelated senses of one word: repeated training, and the business premises of a group of GPs (general practitioners, British family doctors).
explanation.definitionFit: Training drills are what athletes must do, and British doctors call their shared surgery by this same noun.

clue.text: Find fault with old Scot touring Kenya’s borders

indicators.note: a country's borders are its edges, so only the outermost letters are kept
to tour a place is to travel all the way round it, so one piece encircles the other

blocks.note: the Picts were an ancient people of northern Scotland
the first and last letters of Kenya

explanation.surface: A grumbling Scotsman complaining his way around a trip to East Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: The Picts were the ancient inhabitants of north-east Scotland, which is why 'old' is needed; their name is split to take Kenya's edge letters inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To nag or carp at someone over small things is a phrasal verb meaning criticise pettily.

clue.text: A daughter with suitable skills at the outset is flexible

indicators.note: the outset of anything is its very start, so only an opening letter is wanted

blocks.note: taken as printed
d is the standard abbreviation for daughter
apt means fitting or suitable
first letter of skills

explanation.surface: A proud parent praising a versatile daughter who had the right skills from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a verb phrase in the third person, so the answer takes the -S form to match 'is flexible'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who adjusts readily to changing circumstances bends to fit, the same idea as being pliable.

clue.text: Fantasy writer leaving large island split making gift

indicators.note: when something leaves a place it departs, so those letters go missing from the name
split means separated, telling the solver the departing letters are not side by side

blocks.note: J.R.R. Tolkien, author of The Lord of the Rings
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
I is the standard abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A fantasy novelist abandoning a big island that has been divided, producing a present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Split' tells you the two letters removed are not side by side: take the L and the I out separately from TOLKIEN to leave TOKEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A small present given as a symbol of thanks or affection is called a token.

clue.text: Set of cardinals overlooking Latin characteristic of an arch?

indicators.note: to overlook something is to ignore or leave it out, so it disappears

blocks.note: the assembly of cardinals that elects a pope
L is the standard abbreviation for Latin

explanation.surface: Cardinals gazing down from a vantage point over Latin inscriptions on an arch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overlooking' suggests cardinals peering down from a height; here it means ignoring, so the Latin letter drops out of the papal gathering.
explanation.definitionFit: Seen from underneath, an arch curves inward like a hollow, so the question mark flags an example of that shape.

clue.text: Sing country mostly having covered R&B

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the tail is dropped
to cover something is to wrap over it, so one piece goes around the other

blocks.note: Wales, part of the United Kingdom
the letters as printed, ampersand ignored

explanation.surface: A country singer who has mostly recorded cover versions of rhythm and blues songs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covered' is music-business talk for recording someone else's song; here it means wrapping round, so the shortened country goes round RB.
explanation.definitionFit: To trill melodiously, like a songbird, is a lighthearted verb for vocal performance.

clue.text: A job to defend most of reasoning for one making excuses?

indicators.note: most of a word is all but its tail, so the final letter goes
defending means standing guard all round something, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: taken as printed
a post is a position of employment
logic is a system of reasoning

explanation.surface: Someone whose job is to defend weak reasoning on behalf of a person who keeps making excuses.
explanation.walkthrough: The job word surrounds the curtailed reasoning, all after the opening A.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who argues in justification of a cause or person is a defender; the question mark allows the looser excuse-maker sense.

clue.text: Come across vagrant in top in a ragged state

indicators.note: something ragged is torn and disordered, so these letters lose their order

blocks.note: bum is slang for a tramp or down-and-out
five letters of fodder, taken as printed

explanation.surface: Meeting a tramp wearing a tattered shirt on the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In top' looks like describing what the vagrant is wearing, but both words are letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To meet someone by chance is an idiom for encountering them unexpectedly.

clue.text: Outfit with matching elements in musical group

blocks.note: a coordinated set of clothes worn together
a set of performers playing together

explanation.surface: A band all dressed in coordinated outfits.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses share the French root for 'together': coordinated clothing and a group of players.
explanation.definitionFit: A coordinated set of garments and a small band of performers are both called by this borrowed French noun.

clue.text: Excellent witticism in front of guests

indicators.note: the front of a word is where it starts, so only its first letter is kept

blocks.note: a crack is a wisecrack or joke
taken as printed
first letter of guests

explanation.surface: A host delivering a brilliant quip in front of the assembled guests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In front of' reads as one phrase about position; it splits into IN plus 'front of' for the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: British informal praise for something very good; a cracking time is a superb one.

clue.text: Pads, we’re told, for noted detective

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: a pad is slang for a flat or home; the L in the name is silent

explanation.surface: Rumour has it that certain flats are earmarked for a famous sleuth.
explanation.walkthrough: Pad is informal for where someone lives; the plural, spoken, matches the surname of Conan Doyle's fictional sleuth.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherlock, created by Arthur Conan Doyle, is the most famous fictional investigator of all.

clue.text: Go with clubs from the south

indicators.note: in a down entry, reading from the south means reading upward, from bottom to top

blocks.note: bats are the clubs used in cricket or baseball

explanation.surface: A golfer setting off with clubs from the southern end of the course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go' looks like a verb of setting off, but it is the noun for an attempt; the clubs are bats, written upward in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a go and having a stab are both idioms for making an attempt at something.

clue.text: Retainer or nurse kept by a French aunt without English

indicators.note: without means lacking, so that letter is dropped
something kept by another is held inside it, so nurse sits within a French aunt

blocks.note: to nurse someone is to tend them
taken as printed
tante is French for aunt
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A servant or nanny employed by a French aunt who speaks no English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' looks like offering two definitions, but it only joins; the nursing verb sits inside A plus the French aunt once her English letter is gone.
explanation.definitionFit: A retainer is an old word for a servant in a noble household, someone who waits on a master.

clue.text: Element showing no end of remorseless hatred

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so remorseless supplies only its last
no means without, so the selected letter is struck out

blocks.note: a chemical element, symbol Na
final letter of remorseless

explanation.surface: Someone showing endless, unrelenting hatred.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No end of' usually means plenty of; here 'no' removes the last letter of remorseless from the element.
explanation.definitionFit: General loathing or widespread contempt directed at a person is a formal noun for detestation.

clue.text: Extremely arthritic horse in pain

indicators.note: extremes are the outermost points, so only the edge letters are kept

blocks.note: first and last letters of arthritic
first and last letters of horse

explanation.surface: A badly arthritic old horse suffering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' reads as very, but it takes the extremes of both following words.
explanation.definitionFit: A dull continuous hurt is a near synonym for physical suffering or soreness.

clue.text: In merry fashion, cite a free thing used by coffee drinkers

indicators.note: a merry person is tipsy and unsteady, so these letters stagger out of their order

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder, taken as printed

explanation.surface: Someone cheerfully quoting a freebie handed out to café customers.
explanation.walkthrough: A cafetiere is the British name for a French press, a jug whose plunger pushes the grounds down.
explanation.definitionFit: This plunger pot is a piece of kitchen equipment for brewing ground beans, so it serves those who take the hot beverage.

clue.text: Group with knight and bishop backed city

indicators.note: something backed is sent backwards, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: a lot is a set or group
the title given to a knight
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A group including a knight and a bishop supported a city.
explanation.walkthrough: Bristol is a large port city in south-west England. 'Knight and bishop' pulls towards chess, but the knight here is a titled man.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a major urban centre in the west of England, so a proper-noun example of the general term.

clue.text: US singer beginning to upset writer of sweet innocence?

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, the only one kept

blocks.note: the American pop star known by one name
first letter of upset
Bic is a brand of ballpoint pen

explanation.surface: An American singer beginning to upset a songwriter known for sweet, innocent lyrics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' is a person in the surface and a pen in the wordplay; Bic is a ballpoint brand name.
explanation.definitionFit: Resembling a chubby angelic infant describes a face or manner of childlike purity.

clue.text: Haphazardly managed activity in site supplying bread?

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: a cash machine dispenses bread, slang for money
ran a business means managed it
a do is an event or bit of activity

explanation.surface: A chaotic operation at a bakery.
explanation.walkthrough: The bakery reading of 'bread' is the trap: bread is slang for money, so the site is a cash dispenser.
explanation.definitionFit: Done without method or plan, by chance, the adverbial phrase fits anything carried out haphazardly.

clue.text: Loathsome husband developed fault importing drug

indicators.note: to import is to bring something inside, so one piece takes another in
something developed has changed form, so the letters take a new shape

blocks.note: h is the standard abbreviation for husband
five letters of fodder, taken as printed
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A vile husband who developed a habit of bringing drugs into the house.
explanation.walkthrough: The drug letter joins the fault letters and the six are then rearranged after the husband.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that arouses strong dislike or disgust is detestable, a straightforward synonym pair.

clue.text: Secure player in a pack

blocks.note: to fasten something with a key
a second-row forward in a rugby scrum

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pack' suggests cards, but it is the rugby forwards who form the scrum; the second-row forward is a lock.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb for fastening doors shut, and a rugby union forward position in the second row of the scrum.

clue.text: Attractive courtier seen every now and then

indicators.note: seen now and then means seen at intervals, so only every other letter shows

blocks.note: first, third, fifth and seventh letters of courtier

explanation.surface: A handsome royal attendant who appears at court only occasionally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Every now and then' means at regular intervals, so take every other letter starting with the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Pretty or charming in an endearing way; an informal synonym for appealing looks.

clue.text: Burn millions in company lacking solvency

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: Co. is the standard abbreviation for company
m is the abbreviation for million
bust means bankrupt

explanation.surface: A company going bankrupt after burning through millions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Burn' reads as squandering money in the surface, but it is the definition, meaning catch fire.
explanation.definitionFit: To catch fire and be consumed by flames is the literal sense of this chemistry verb.

clue.text: Fewest points admitted by imam in imamate

indicators.note: something admitted by others is let in among them, so it sits inside their letters

blocks.note: runs across the last letter of imam, all of in, and the start of imamate

explanation.surface: A religious leader in their own jurisdiction conceding the lowest score.
explanation.walkthrough: An imamate is the territory or office of an imam; the answer straddles three words.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural of the mathematical term for the lowest value on a curve or smallest amounts reached.

clue.text: African party cuts notice for spirited session?

indicators.note: something that cuts into another splits it apart and lodges in the gap

blocks.note: to notice is to see
the African National Congress, South Africa's governing party

explanation.surface: A political party slashing publicity for a lively meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notice' looks like a noun, a poster or announcement; it is the verb. 'Spirited' is the pun: a session involving spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: A gathering where people try to contact the dead is a meeting full of ghosts, hence the playful question mark.

clue.text: Slate rubbish about central part of case

indicators.note: the central part of a word is its middle, so the outer letters go
about means around, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: rot means nonsense
the middle two letters of case

explanation.surface: Someone dismissing the core of a legal argument as nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slate' is British informal for criticise harshly, not the roofing stone; the answer has the same meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to criticise someone severely or tear into them in public.

clue.text: Evict a mob in a riot, being antagonistic?

indicators.note: a riot is wild disorder, so these letters are thrown into confusion

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder, taken as printed

explanation.surface: Police clearing a rioting crowd and getting hostile about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a riot' fits the scene of a mob so well that it hides its job of reordering letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Eager to fight or argue; hostile and ready for conflict are shared meanings of these adjectives.

clue.text: A film about source of sweet or savoury jelly

indicators.note: a source is where something starts, so only the first letter is wanted
about means around, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: A as printed, plus pic, informal for a film
first letter of sweet

explanation.surface: A documentary about where sweet or savoury jellies come from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet or savoury jelly' wants to be one definition, but sweet belongs to the wordplay; aspic is only the savoury kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A clear gelatin made from meat stock, used to set cold dishes, is a savoury moulded preparation.

clue.text: Move end of project to get financial allowance

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, the only one kept

blocks.note: to budge is to shift slightly
last letter of project

explanation.surface: Postponing a project's deadline to secure more funding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Move end of project' reads as rescheduling a deadline; it splits into the verb plus a final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The sum of money set aside for a purpose is the amount one is permitted to spend.

clue.text: Sense politician is enthralled by free outing

indicators.note: letters set free are loose to move into a new arrangement
one enthralled by something is captured and held by it, so the politician is held inside

blocks.note: six letters of fodder, taken as printed
Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician delighted by a complimentary day trip, a junket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free outing' reads as a perk; 'free' is the instruction to rearrange the outing letters around the politician.
explanation.definitionFit: Practical shrewdness or common sense, often with a hint of initiative, is an informal synonym.

clue.text: Curve hard to miss in part of a legislature

indicators.note: to miss something is to be without it, so that letter goes

blocks.note: a house of parliament, such as the upper chamber
h is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A bend that is hard to overlook inside a parliament building.
explanation.walkthrough: Camber is the slight arch across a road surface, higher in the middle so water drains off.
explanation.definitionFit: A gentle convex slope or bow, as on a road or a ship's deck, is a technical word for a shallow bend.

clue.text: Conventional poster close to fine wooden barrier

indicators.note: the close of a word is its ending, so the final letter is kept

blocks.note: a stock response is a standard, conventional one
an ad is an advertisement, such as a poster
last letter of fine

explanation.surface: An ordinary advertising hoarding placed near a fine timber fence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to' reads as near; here it means the closing letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A defensive enclosure of upright timber posts is a fortified fence made of logs.
